newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH FUEL PRICE RISE IMPACT ON CPI SEEN LIMITED.
newsitem.headline: POLISH FUEL PRICE RISE IMPACT ON CPI SEEN LIMITED.

text.p: The rise of official maximum prices of diesel fuel and petrol as of October 9 is likely to have only a limited impact on overall monthly consumer price growth, analysts said on Friday.

They said the 0.7 percent rise in officially controlled maximum retail petrol prices and a 4.9 percent rise in diesel prices would likely add up to one percentage point to this month's growth in consumer prices.
"The fuel rise is sure to have some, though not big, impact on other prices because fuel is the bloodstream of the economy," said Jaroslaw Krzesniak, analyst at the Polish Development Bank SA.
"I think the move finally buries the government's 17 percent year-on-year inflation target for this year making a figure well above 19 percent much more realistic," he said.
Poland's top 25 banks expect the year-on-year consumer price index to ease to about 18.7 percent in December from 21.6 percent in December 1995.
Economists said the inflationary impulse from the rise would likely be dampened by the quickly growing imports of consumer goods.

"The price rise was long called for. Such moves usually are a good excuse to raise prices of other consumer goods but the temptation is likely to be limited by competitive imports," an economist from an independent institute, who asked not to be named, said.
"I would not expect the fuel rise to add more than one percent to the overall monthly CPI," he said.
Economists noted the fuel price rise was accompanied by a simultaneous cut in the excise tax on diesel fuel.

"The simultaneous lowering of the excise tax shows the government is trying very hard to limit its potential impact on the consumer price index," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst of the Planning Ministry.
The finance ministry cut the excise tax on both imported and domestically produced diesel by 60 zlotys to 400 zlotys and 360 zlotys respectively from October 9 until the end of the year.

But analysts said the ministry's decision on the rise, difficult in the context of its ambitious inflation goals, was only a half-measure, which proved a full near-term liberalisation of fuel prices was necessary.

"The finance ministry has long been delaying the fuel price rise to meet the inflation target at all costs. Had fuel prices been freed earlier...the market would better adjust to them," said Bohdan Wyznikiewicz of the indpendent Gdansk economic think tank.
